name: Dahlia
handling: Deadhead deep and often. Runs to frost, then cut to four inches and mulch.
idNote: Cultivar unknown. Worth naming if you ever want to reorder the same one.

name: Gaillardia
handling: Deadhead relentlessly. Dies of wet feet here, never of cold, so keep the crown dry and open.

name: Scabiosa
handling: Deadhead. Will run into November here.

name: Cosmos
handling: Deadhead. Let a few set seed to self-sow.

name: Sunflower
handling: Leave heads for birds, or cut when the back turns brown. The side bed plants have powdery mildew: strip the worst leaves, bin them rather than composting, and do not spray this late.
idNote: The dark red one is likely 'Velvet Queen' or 'Chocolate', but that is a guess from colour alone.

name: Echinacea
handling: Leave seedheads standing all winter for goldfinches. Cut in March.

name: Echinacea
handling: Same as the purple. Leave standing, cut in March.
idNote: Definitely a white echinacea. Which cultivar is a guess, and it only matters for reordering.

name: Gladiolus
handling: Spike off now, leaves stay until fully yellow. Overwinters in these beds already. Inspect each corm when lifting and spreading in fall.
idNote: Confirmed as present. See the crocosmia entry for whether every strap-leaved clump is actually a glad.

name: California poppy
handling: Self-sows freely. Leave it to do that.

name: Shirley poppy
handling: Shake pods where you want them, then pull the plants. Will not transplant and resents spring sowing.

name: Snapdragon
handling: Cut spent spikes, leave the plants. Often overwinters here and returns. Let a few spikes shatter if you want more.

name: Oregano
handling: Shear a third off now and dry the leaves. Hard prune into old wood in spring, not in fall.

name: Hardy geranium
handling: Shear to a few inches for fresh foliage and often a second flush of flowers.

name: Whorled spike plant
handling: Leave the seed spikes standing either way. Only veronica gives a second flush if you cut them now.
idNote: Roll the stem: square with four flat sides means agastache, round means veronica. Then count leaves at one joint: two facing each other is agastache, three or more radiating like spokes is Culver's root. Best guess from photos is Culver's root.

name: Silver-grey dried mound
handling: Do not pull until identified. Squeeze a stem at the base: brittle and hollow means dead, flexible and green inside means alive.
idNote: A large mass of fine grey branching stems. Candidates are artemisia, lavender, statice, or simply a spent annual. Crush a stem and smell it, then photograph the base of the plant where it meets the soil, and whether it has a woody trunk or many soft stems.

name: Small blue flowers
handling: Harmless either way. Identify before deciding whether it returns next year.
idNote: Tiny blue-purple flowers on thin wiry stems threading through Street Bed 1. Lobelia is a low sprawling annual with tiny fan-shaped flowers. Salvia stands upright with flowers in tiers up a spike. A close photo of a single flower settles it.

name: Round-leaved plant
handling: If nasturtium, it is an annual, edible, and will self-sow.
idNote: Nasturtium leaves are round like small lily pads with the stem joining in the middle of the leaf rather than at the edge. That centre-join is the giveaway.

name: Small white daisy
handling: If feverfew, it self-sows enthusiastically and you may want to limit it.
idNote: Small white daisies with yellow centres. Feverfew has divided, slightly yellow-green foliage and a strong bitter smell when crushed.

name: Possible crocosmia
handling: If present, keep it separate when lifting. Crocosmia spreads by underground corm chains and will colonise a bed.
idNote: Out of bloom the two look nearly identical. Gladiolus leaves are thicker, stiffer and stand upright in a flat fan. Crocosmia leaves are thinner, more pleated and arch over. The real tell is underground: a gladiolus corm sits alone with small cormels around its base, while crocosmia forms a vertical chain of corms stacked on top of each other. You will see it when you lift them this fall.

name: Strawberry
handling: Do not mow the foliage. Thin the mat to about one plant every six to eight inches, pinch off runners you do not want, and let a few root as replacements.
idNote: Flowering and fruiting at the end of August means everbearing or day-neutral, not June-bearing. That matters because the two get opposite fall treatment. Confirm by whether it also gave you a heavy single crop in June.

name: Beans
handling: Keep picking, which is what keeps them producing. When finished, cut at soil level and leave the roots in the ground for the nitrogen in the nodules.
idNote: Purple flowers point to a purple-podded variety. Whether these are bush or pole changes nothing about care but is worth noting for next year. A photo of a pod would settle it.

name: Dark puckered greens
handling: All three are edible and all three can be picked leaf by leaf, so it is safe to harvest either way.
idNote: Growing low among the beans, deeply savoyed dark leaves. Chard has a thick white or coloured midrib and stalk. Beet has a reddish stalk and a swelling root at the base. Spinach has thin plain stalks and no swollen root. Look at the stalk colour and scrape the soil at the base.

name: Low creeping ground cover
handling: Weed it out now either way, before it seeds or spreads further into the strawberry mat.
idNote: Small round leaves running along the soil between the strawberries. Chickweed is soft, shallow-rooted and pulls out in mats, and is a minor annual nuisance. Ground ivy has scalloped leaves, a square stem, a strong minty smell when crushed, and roots at every node, and it is a genuine long-term problem. Crush a leaf and roll the stem: this one is worth knowing.
